title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 119
paragraphs: In the other cities also, those placed in charge of the business reckoned roughly the same cost. For the dinner was arranged as follows, having been ordered a long time in advance and reckoned a matter of the greatest importance. In the first place, as soon as they heard of it from the heralds who carried the proclamation around, the citizens in each city distributed grain among their households, and everyone kept grinding wheat and barley meal for many months. Then they fattened cattle, finding and obtaining the finest animals at a high price, and they kept birds both of the land and of the water in cages or in pools, all for the entertainment of the army. Then again they had drinking-cups and mixing-bowls made of gold and silver, and all the other table service; these were made for the king himself and for those who dined with him, but for the rest of the army only the appointed rations were provided. When the army came to any place, a tent was already pitched ready in which Xerxes himself took his rest, while the rest of the army stayed in the open air. When dinner-time came, it was the hosts who had to toil; while the others, once they had eaten their fill and passed the night there, the next day tore down the tent, took all the movable furniture with them, and moved on, leaving nothing behind.
